resources.string: Starting Picket\'s privileged helper through Shizuku.
Picket needs Shizuku (or Sui on rooted devices) to see other apps\' processes and settings. Install Shizuku, start it, then come back.
Shizuku stops when the phone restarts. Open Shizuku and start it again; with wireless debugging you may have to pair it again after a reboot.
This Shizuku version does not support the helper service Picket uses. Update Shizuku and try again.
Picket runs a small helper with shell privileges through Shizuku. It can only do the specific things listed in the app, never run arbitrary commands, and Picket has no internet access.
You chose not to be asked again. Open Shizuku, find Picket in the list of authorised apps and allow it.

Why Shizuku? Android hides other apps\' processes, services and privileged settings from normal apps. Shizuku lends Picket the same rights you have in an adb shell, without rooting the phone.

Shizuku, the helper process, and why there is no internet permission
True black backgrounds in dark mode, for OLED screens.
Subtle confirmations for toggles and actions. Never while scrolling.

Android does not let normal apps see other apps\' processes or privileged settings. Shizuku runs a small server with the rights of the adb shell (or root, if you use Sui) and lends them to apps you approve.
Picket asks Shizuku to start a helper, \"app.brokoli5191.picket:privileged\", which runs with those rights. It stops when Picket stops and only answers Picket.

The helper cannot run arbitrary commands. It knows a fixed list of operations, checks every package and component name it receives, and runs each command as a list of arguments, never through a shell. Before any change you see the exact command line.
A tool with shell rights should not be able to send data anywhere. Picket does not request the internet permission, and its build fails if anything tries to add it.
Shizuku does not survive a restart. Start it again from the Shizuku app; with wireless debugging you may need to pair again.
Android blocks sideloaded apps from getting notification or accessibility access through Settings. When Picket undoes a revocation it restores that access through the shell, which works even then.

Ends all of the app\'s processes and puts it into the stopped state: no alarms, jobs or broadcasts reach it until it is opened again. There is nothing to undo; the app starts normally the next time you open it.
Ends the app\'s background processes the way Android does when memory runs low. Foreground work is left alone, and the app may start again at any time.
Asks Android to stop this one service. A service that another app is bound to, or that runs in the foreground, may keep running; force stop is the fallback.
The app stops receiving your notifications. Undo grants the access again.
Removes only this service from the enabled accessibility services and leaves the others on. Undo restores the previous list exactly.
The app can no longer change Do Not Disturb. Undo grants the access again.
The app stops being the default for this role, and Android may ask you to choose another one. Undo makes it the default again.
Sets the app op to ignore. Undo restores the previous mode.
Blocks background activity while you are not using the app: background services, jobs and alarms stop. Undo allows it again.
Puts the app into the most limited standby bucket, where jobs and alarms run about once a day. Android may move it to another bucket on its own later. Undo restores the previous bucket.
The app is subject to Doze and battery optimisation again. Undo adds the exemption back.
Revokes this runtime permission. Android ends the app\'s processes when a permission is taken away. Undo grants it again.
Disables the app for this user: it disappears from the launcher and cannot run until it is enabled again. Undo restores its previous state.
This is a system app. Disabling system packages can leave One UI or the whole phone unusable, up to boot loops or a missing launcher or keyboard. Only continue if you know what this package does.
Opens the matching screen in Android\'s Settings. Picket runs nothing for this.
There is no undo for this.
Undone through the shell. That works even where Settings blocks a sideloaded app (restricted setting).
Android 13 and later may refuse to turn this back on in Settings if the app was sideloaded (restricted setting). Undo in Picket restores it through the shell.
